author: deep
title: Use-after-free into __free_hook
body: The note service frees a note but keeps its pointer, so editing that note afterwards writes into memory the allocator has already recycled. Reading the stale note printed a pointer from the unsorted bin, which sits at a fixed offset inside the C runtime library, so subtracting that offset gave us the library base. With the base known we poisoned the tcache free list so the next malloc returned a chunk on top of __free_hook, wrote system() there, and freed a note containing /bin/sh to get a shell.

author: arjun
title: Double free and tcache poisoning
body: Deleting the same note twice puts one chunk on the tcache list twice. We used that double free to overwrite the next pointer, made malloc hand back a chunk inside the GOT, and replaced free with puts to print a resolved function pointer. That gave the base of glibc; a second round of poisoning pointed free at a one_gadget and the next delete spawned a shell.

author: meera
title: UAF to overwrite __free_hook
body: The note service frees a note but keeps its pointer, so editing the note afterwards writes into memory that the allocator has already recycled. Reading the stale note printed an unsorted bin pointer, which sits at a fixed offset inside the C runtime library, and subtracting that offset gave us the library base. Once the base was known we poisoned the tcache free list so that the next malloc returned a chunk on top of __free_hook, wrote system() into it, and freed a note containing /bin/sh to get our shell.

author: kabir
title: Forging the session cookie
body: The session cookie is a JSON Web Token, and the server trusts whatever algorithm the header names. Changing alg to none and stripping the signature was rejected, but switching from RS256 to HS256 and signing with the public key, which the site serves at /jwks.json, was accepted as valid. We set role to admin in the payload and the admin panel showed the flag.

author: arjun
title: Algorithm confusion on the session token
body: Decoding the cookie showed an RS256 JWT. The verifier accepted HS256 tokens and used the RSA public key as the HMAC secret, so we fetched the public key, re-signed a token with is_admin set to true using HS256, and replaced our cookie. The dashboard then rendered the administrator view with the flag in the page footer.

author: rhea
title: Byte-at-a-time against ECB
body: The service encrypts our input followed by the secret under AES in ECB mode, so equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks. We sent fifteen filler bytes so that the first unknown byte fell at the end of a block, recorded that block, and then tried all 256 values for the last byte until the block matched. Repeating with one fewer filler byte each time recovered the secret one character at a time.

author: priya
title: Chosen-prefix block matching
body: Sending a long run of the same letter produced repeating ciphertext blocks, which confirmed the electronic codebook mode and a sixteen byte block. Because the flag is appended to our prefix, we built a dictionary of ciphertext blocks for every possible final byte and looked up the real block in it. Shifting the alignment by one byte per round decrypted the whole suffix without ever learning the key.

author: ishaan
title: Recovering the deleted partition
body: The disk image had an empty partition table, but scanning for file system signatures found an ext4 superblock about one gigabyte in. We rebuilt the partition entry at that offset and mounted it read only. The directory listing showed nothing interesting, but the journal still referenced a removed zip file, and extracting it from its inode gave an archive with the flag inside a text file.

author: zoya
title: File carving from unallocated space
body: Instead of repairing the partition we ran a carver over the raw image and pulled out everything with a known header. Among a few hundred JPEGs there was one PKZIP archive that had been deleted before the partition was removed. The archive was not encrypted and contained notes.txt, whose last line was the flag.

author: deep
title: Format string leak, then overflow
body: The guestbook passes the visitor name directly to printf, so a name made of %p specifiers prints values from the stack. The fifteenth value always ended in 00, which is the stack canary, and a nearby value was a return address that revealed the binary base. The comment field then overflows a 64 byte buffer: we wrote the filler, the leaked canary unchanged, a saved frame pointer, and a short chain that calls the win function.

author: ananya
title: Bypassing the stack protector with %p
body: Stack smashing protection stops a plain overflow because the cookie before the return address is checked on exit. The program has a second bug, an uncontrolled format string, and with it we dumped the stack and read the cookie value for the current process. Putting the same cookie back in our overflow payload keeps the check happy, and the return address after it sends execution into system with a pointer to /bin/sh.

author: vikram
title: ret2libc in two stages
body: The binary has a non-executable stack and no useful functions of its own, so shellcode is out. In the first stage our chain called puts with the address of a GOT entry and returned to main, which printed where puts lives in libc. From that we computed the address of system and of the /bin/sh string, and the second stage called system with a pop rdi gadget. A single extra ret was needed to keep the stack sixteen byte aligned.

author: ira
title: Return oriented programming against NX
body: With data execution prevention on, the overflow can only reuse code that already exists. We leaked the load address of the C library by printing a resolved import, then returned into the vulnerable function again. Knowing the library base, we built a return oriented chain that sets the first argument register and jumps to execve, which gave an interactive shell to read flag.txt.

author: dev
title: One null byte to move the frame
body: The copy loop writes one byte past the name buffer, and that byte is the terminating zero, which lands on the least significant byte of the saved frame pointer. When the caller returns it restores a frame pointer that now points lower, into the middle of our buffer, and its own return address is read from there. We filled the buffer with repeated ret gadgets followed by the real chain, so wherever the pivot landed it slid into our code.

author: rhea
title: UNION based injection on the search box
body: A single quote in the station search produced a database error, so the input is concatenated into the query. ORDER BY 4 failed and ORDER BY 3 worked, which means three columns. A UNION SELECT of three literals showed that the second column is printed, and from the catalog we listed the tables and found one called secrets. Selecting its value column through the union printed the flag in the timetable.

author: sana
title: Dumping a hidden table through the timetable
body: The timetable filter is injectable: closing the string and adding a comment returns every row. We found the column count by adding NULLs to a UNION until the error went away, then replaced one NULL with a query against information_schema to enumerate table names. The table that the application never displays had a single row, and reading it through the same union gave us the flag.

author: diya
title: Dumping the hidden table via the timetable
body: The timetable filter is injectable: closing the string and adding a comment returns all rows. We found the column count by adding NULLs to a UNION until the error disappeared, then replaced one NULL with a query against information_schema to enumerate the table names. The table that the application never displays had one row, and reading it through the same union gave us the flag.

author: aditya
title: Server-side template injection
body: Entering seven times seven inside double curly braces as the recipient name printed 49 on the card, so the name is rendered as a template on the server. From an empty string we walked up to its class, then to object, and listed all subclasses that the interpreter had loaded. One of them wraps process creation, and calling it with cat on the flag file put the flag in the rendered greeting.

author: deep
title: Escaping the template sandbox
body: The card generator blocks the words import and os, but it still evaluates expressions in the name field. We reached the built-in functions through the globals of a function object that the template context exposes, and built the blocked names by joining shorter strings. That let us open the flag file and read it directly into the page.

author: lakshmi
title: Directory traversal past a weak filter
body: The viewer takes a file parameter and joins it to the uploads directory. Dot dot slash is removed from the input, but only once, so writing the sequence nested inside itself leaves a working traversal after the filter has run. Going up one level and asking for flag.txt returned the file.

author: rohan
title: Reading files outside the web root
body: Requesting a document that does not exist showed the full path in the error message, so we knew the uploads folder sits one level below the application root. The traversal filter looks for the literal characters, and encoding the slash as a percent sequence got past it. The parent directory contained the flag file next to the application source.

author: sana
title: Time-based blind injection
body: The login page answers every request with the same message, so there is no visible difference between true and false. Adding a conditional sleep to the username made the response take five seconds only when the condition held, which gives one bit per request. We binary searched each character of the administrator password hash using the response time, about seven requests per character, and submitted the recovered hash as the flag.

author: karthik
title: Cube root attack on textbook RSA
body: The public exponent is three and the message has no padding. The plaintext is about forty bytes, so its cube is smaller than the 2048 bit modulus and the modular reduction never happens. The ciphertext is therefore just the message cubed as an ordinary integer, and taking an exact integer cube root with a big number library gave the plaintext directly.

author: rhea
title: When RSA is only a power function
body: With e equal to 3 and a short unpadded message, encryption does not wrap around n. We computed the integer cube root of c using Newton iteration on arbitrary precision integers, checked that cubing the result gave back c exactly, and converted the number to bytes to read the flag. No factoring was needed.

author: priya
title: Crib dragging two ciphertexts
body: Both messages were encrypted with the same keystream, so XORing the ciphertexts removes the key and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts. We slid common English words across that combined text; wherever the guess was right, the other message showed readable letters at the same position. Extending the readable fragments in both directions recovered both sentences, and the second one contained the flag.

author: nisha
title: Keystream reuse in a stream cipher
body: A one time pad is only secure if the pad is used once. Here the nonce is repeated, so the two ciphertexts share a keystream. Since we were told one plaintext is an English sentence, we guessed it started with a capital letter and the word The, recovered the first bytes of the keystream from that guess, and decrypted the start of the other message. Repeating the guess and check loop revealed everything.

author: karthik
title: Padding oracle on CBC cookies
body: The server returns a different status code when the PKCS7 padding of a decrypted cookie is invalid, which is enough to decrypt without the key. For each block we changed the last byte of the preceding block until the padding was accepted, which reveals one byte of the intermediate value, then adjusted it to force padding of two and moved left. About two thousand requests per block decrypted the administrator cookie, and the same oracle let us encrypt a cookie of our own choosing.

author: deep
title: Length extension on a prefix MAC
body: The request signature is the SHA-256 of a secret followed by the query string. Because the digest is the internal state of the hash after the last block, we can load that state and keep hashing without knowing the secret. We appended the original padding and then the admin parameter, computed the new digest from the old one, and tried secret lengths from eight to thirty two until the server accepted the request.

author: priya
title: Why secret-prefix hashing is not a MAC
body: Merkle Damgard hashes let anyone who knows hash(m) compute hash(m plus padding plus suffix). The API authenticates with hash(key concatenated with message), so we extended a valid message with an extra field that grants administrator rights and produced a matching tag. The only unknown was the key length, which changes the padding, and brute forcing it took sixteen attempts. HMAC would have prevented this.

author: neel
title: DNS tunnelling in the capture
body: Filtering the capture for DNS showed hundreds of queries for long random looking subdomains of a single domain, far more than normal browsing would create. Each label started with a counter and the rest was base32 text. We extracted the query names, sorted them by the counter, joined the encoded parts, and decoded them into a gzip file that contained the stolen document with the flag.

author: rhea
title: Exfiltration hidden in name lookups
body: The web traffic in the pcap was clean, but one host sent an unusual volume of name resolution requests to a server that is not the configured resolver. The requested names carry the data: a sequence number, then a chunk of encoded payload. Reassembling the chunks in order and decoding them recovered a compressed archive, and the flag was in the only file inside.

author: zoya
title: Pulling a secret from a memory image
body: We identified the image as a Windows 10 build and listed the running processes, which included the password manager. Dumping the memory of that process and searching for the marker that precedes the unlocked database key found it in two places on the heap. Using the key to open the vault file that was also cached in memory showed an entry whose password was the flag.

author: nisha
title: GPS coordinates in the photo metadata
body: The photograph still had its EXIF block, including the GPS latitude and longitude written by the phone. Converting the degrees, minutes and seconds to decimal degrees and rounding to four places gave the password in the format the challenge described. The archive opened with it and held the flag.

author: om
title: Geotag as an archive password
body: Running a metadata reader over the image printed the camera model, the time, and a geotag. The description said the location was the key, so we tried the coordinates as the zip password: first as degrees and minutes, which failed, and then as decimal numbers separated by a comma, which worked.

author: tara
title: Reversing the key check loop
body: The success string is referenced from one function, and that function loops over the input comparing each transformed character with a constant table. The transform is an exclusive or of the character with its position. Applying the same operation to the table gives the expected input, which is a twenty character licence key, and the program printed the flag when given it.

author: sameer
title: Solving the crackme statically
body: We opened the binary in a disassembler and followed the cross reference from the wrong key message. The comparison is done byte by byte against data stored in the read only section after a simple reversible encoding. Writing five lines of script to undo the encoding produced a valid serial without running the program at all.

author: tara
title: Patching out the debugger checks
body: The program calls ptrace on itself at start and exits if that fails, and it also reads the timestamp counter twice and bails out if too many cycles passed between the reads. We replaced the conditional jumps after both checks with no operation instructions and ran the patched binary under a debugger. A breakpoint after the decryption routine showed the flag in the output buffer.

author: ananya
title: Lifting a nested virtual machine
body: The executable is an interpreter with a fetch, decode, execute loop and about twenty opcodes. After writing a disassembler for it we saw that the bytecode was itself another, smaller interpreter running a third program that validates the input. We lifted both layers into ordinary expressions, which turned the check into a set of linear equations over bytes, and a constraint solver produced the flag.

author: varun
title: A secret left in the commit history
body: The current tree had nothing sensitive, but the log showed a commit titled remove config. Showing the patch of the commit before it printed the configuration file with an API key in it. The flag was that key: deleting a file in a later commit does not remove it from history.

author: deep
title: Recovering a deleted branch
body: Nothing in the visible history contained a key, so we listed the reflog and the unreachable objects. One dangling commit belonged to a branch that had been deleted, and its tree contained a private key file. Checking that commit out by its hash recovered the file and the flag inside its comment line.
